title: Review: Old Soul Tintype Series #3 Bourbon

The post Review: Old Soul Tintype Series #3 Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Old Soul bourbon comes from the Cathead Distillery in Jackson, Mississippi, but the whiskey in the Tintype series is sourced entirely from Indiana. It is then sent to Mississippi where it is aged. Today we are trying the third in the Tintype Series. I had a chance to try the previous two installments, and they were serious bourbons showcasing depth and complexity at cask strength.

The Tintype Series showcases blues artists, and each entry includes a distinctive tintype image of a notable musician on the front of the bottle. Tintype #1 presented an image of Captain Luke Mayer. Tintype #2 had Hermon Hitson. Tintype #3 has a really cool picture of blues slide guitarist Kenny Brown.

The whiskey in all of the Tintype bourbons has the same source and location for aging, but they are otherwise quite different from one another, with different mash bills and different age statements. The one we are trying today is 60% corn, 36% rye, and 4% malted barley, and it was aged for 11 years. That’s a lot of rye and a lengthy period of time in Mississippi’s hot humid weather, which should have encouraged vigorous interaction with the cask. Let’s pour a glass and give it a try.

Old Soul Tintype Series #3 Straight Bourbon Whiskey Review

Right out of the gate, this is an enticing whiskey offering a lovely and complex nose that showcases aromas of chewy caramel, maple syrup, vanilla, butterscotch pudding, crème brûlée, and a bit of leather. It might sound overly sweet, however the notes don’t jumble together but rather take turns coming to the fore, with wood tannins joining in to offer a counterbalance.

On the palate, the bourbon follows the nose beautifully. Each of the notes come through with clarity and then plays together nicely with the other flavors. Bold caramel melts into butterscotch pudding then becomes maple syrup and finally transforms into the burnt sugar on crème brûlée as soft leather sits in the background. The alcohol provides a bit of a bite, but it isn’t overwhelming as the flavors flit back and forth, creating a complex character, finally leading into a long, gentle finish as the flavors evaporate. I was really quite taken with this bourbon. I enjoyed both of the previous tintype whiskeys, but this is my favorite of the three.

103.5 proof.

A / $135 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Whiskeys of Lasso Motel (Updated 2026)
summary:
So there may not be an actual Lasso Motel, but it does serve as a fun moniker for a new operation that’s sourcing, finishing, and bottling whiskey — and lots of it. By my count the company has 13 different whiskeys on the market now — mostly bourbon but also a rye and a few…

The post Review: Whiskeys of Lasso Motel (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
So there may not be an actual Lasso Motel, but it does serve as a fun moniker for a new operation that’s sourcing, finishing, and bottling whiskey — and lots of it. By my count the company has 13 different whiskeys on the market now — mostly bourbon but also a rye and a few other oddities. Lasso Motel is surprisingly transparent about all of its sourcing, revealing the origins of each of its 13 bottles — and they’re not all from the same producer.

The creation of Lasso Motel Whiskey was inspired by president Devin Odell’s time at the storied Belmont Hotel—a now-shuttered but historic Dallas landmark reminiscent of the iconic Chateau Marmont. The hotel, once a vibrant hub for artists and celebrities, offered stunning views of the city. Encapsulated by the rock-and-roll nostalgia and the sense of history that the Belmont represented, Odell’s memories of this place laid the foundation for the timeless essence of Lasso Motel Whiskey.

“Lasso Motel Whiskey began as a passion project of mine and pays homage to the whiskey industry. While many brands draw on stories of prohibition or the Old West, we chose a product and packaging design that reflects our own style and experience. The result is a whiskey that not only shines in a glass but also stands out on a bar top. Distinguished by its heavy-grade glass decanter and paperweight cork, Lasso Motel Whiskey offers a premium consumer experience, featuring a range of global cask selections that make each bottle a coveted addition to any collection,” says Devin Odell of Dynasty Spirits. “Lasso Motel Whiskey is driven by our commitment to constant innovation and a dedication to creating unique consumer experiences. Lasso will continue to evolve, offering new products that resonate with both whiskey enthusiasts and casual drinkers alike.”

Recently we got a box with all 13 whiskeys in it, which took weeks to properly sift through. But we did, and we have thoughts.

Update 2026: We’re adding additional Lasso Motel coverage as new expressions arrive.

Lasso Motel Bourbon Cognac Cask Finish Review

Distilled by Green River: 70% corn, 21% rye, 9% malted barley. No age statement, but finished in Cognac casks. Soft and pretty on the nose, evoking florals first, then caramel and grittier barrel char notes, as the hints of Cognac fade away. The palate is again quite gentle and easy, evoking a soft milk chocolate quality, chased by hints of raisins, baking spice, and lavender — the lattermost especially evident on the finish. The Cognac finishing here comes off as awfully restrained, which isn’t a dig. However the underlying whiskey feels a little underdeveloped, too. Agreeable, never rocking the boat. 100 proof. B+ / $70 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Lasso Motel Bourbon Mizunara Cask Finish Review

Green River bourbon distillate, same mashbill. No age statement, finished in Japanese mizunara oak casks. Clear mizunara notes start things off on the nose, making for a savory, mushroomy, umami quality that moves from bacon fat to roasted hazelnut notes after getting some air. A big, chewy palate doubles down on nuts, showcasing a well-peppered core that evokes flavors of barrel char and burnt popcorn. Dark chocolate emerges as the more savory elements fade, finishing on a sustained, toasted oak note that never comes across as overdone. Caramel overtones temper the savoriness with time in glass, making for a whiskey that really evolves and grows on you as it develops. 100 proof. A- / $70

Lasso Motel Bourbon Rose Cask Finish Review

Green River bourbon, same mash as above. No age statement, finished in French rose wine casks. There aren’t a lot of them out there, but I don’t know if I’ve ever been disappointed in a rose-finished whiskey. This one’s a lot more evocative of rose wine than Penelope’s, offering a fruity and floral note that evokes the finishing barrel right away. Strawberry and orange blossom notes are effusive both on the nose and on the palate, which is embarrassingly sweet and not in a bad way. Vanilla cream and milk chocolate covered strawberries dominate, then a gently tannic quality comes into focus, evoking the initial charred barrel and tempering things before sugar takes over. The spray of aromatic pink flowers on the finish is simply delightful; possibly the best whiskey in this lineup. 100 proof. A / $70

Lasso Motel Bourbon Le Stave Review

Green River bourbon (see above), no age statement, finished with French oak staves (not in French oak barrels). This whiskey has a softer touch that tempers its attack and causes it to come across as really quite harmless. A gentle note of anise is evident on the nose, along with a toastier note of sesame and some earthy honey. A brown butter quality develops in short order, and that’s equally evident on the palate, which is just as easygoing with its evocation of butter cookies, Cheerios, and some gentle cinnamon notes. To call this whiskey thin wouldn’t be entirely accurate, but it does have more in common with Canadian whiskey than I ever thought possible in a bourbon. 100 proof. B / $70 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Lasso Motel Bourbon Amburana Cask Finish Review

Green River bourbon, finished in Brazilian amburana casks previously used for cachaca. Amburana makes for a divisive impact on whiskey, and this expression is perhaps an ideal exemplar of that. Overwhelming spice and incense attack the nose here, giving the whiskey aromatics that range from gingerbread to saffron to patchouli. The cinnamon notes are extreme to a fault, and if you’re not ready for it, this Amburana Cask offering can wallop you with its spice bill. Flavors of unctuous cinnamon rolls meld with grandma’s perfume to create a potpourri experience, infused with the inimitable (and hard to describe) amburana-driven qualities of marzipan, cloves, pepper, and heavily toasted coconut. Somehow equally sweet, savory, and spicy, it’s an utter mind-scrambler that I could never fully wrap my head around. Which is why people don’t like amburana, I get it. 100 proof. B / $70 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Lasso Motel Bourbon Port Cask Finish Review

Green River juice finished in a Tawny Port wine cask. You catch the sweet Port influence right from the start: The nose has some of that cereal punch, but it’s laden with sweet raisin elements, alongside a healthy note of cinnamon and warming ginger — then some black pepper as things develop further with airtime. The palate does not rock the boat, though there’s a more aggressive clove character and a bite of sarsaparilla — leaving behind a racy coating of spices. The finish really hits like a warm Dr Pepper, which is a tasting note I can’t say I’ve ever used. Fortunately I really like Dr Pepper, and since I no longer drink soda…. 100 proof. A- / $70

Lasso Motel Bourbon Sherry Cask Finish Review

You surely saw this one coming: Green River bourbon with a Pedro Ximenez cask finish — not oloroso. Aggressive sherry on the nose — bold with with that sweet and oxidized PX character, obvious from the get-go. A mix of seasoned nuts and macerated berries makes the underlying bourbon largely unparseable, save for a vague barrel char note and a slick of licorice evident. I was expecting something less than thrilling on the tongue, but the palate is rich and enveloping, and the PX really works well here. Gentle chocolate notes pair with prune, orange peel, and a heavy baking spice complement to create a finished product that is certainly dessert-adjacent but not bruisingly so. The finish fires up a curiously Eastern character, hinting at white pepper, saffron, and turmeric. Exotic, fun, and very rich. 100 proof. A- / $70

Lasso Motel Bourbon Tokaji Cask Finish Review

Green River bourbon finished on Hungarian Tokaji barrels. One of the sweetest and most exuberant whiskeys in the Lasso Motel lineup, this bourbon lets the Tokaji take the reins, and in glorious fashion. Sweet notes of golden raisins percolate a floral and lightly citrus-touched nose, with a note of white pepper adding a touch of intrigue. The flower petals are even more intense on the palate, which evokes rose water and lilacs, increasingly perfumed as it develops in the glass. Sweet notes of dried plums, more golden raisins, and orange blossom honey make for an appropriately dessert-like conclusion — complete with late-game notes of chocolate and cinnamon. More complex than you think, but just as delightful. 100 proof. A / $70 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Lasso Motel Bourbon Naranja Cask Finish Review

The last of the finished Green River bourbons, this expression is finished in Spanish vino de naranja casks — white wine infused with orange peel. There’s no shortage of citrus on the nose here, not just navel orange but also grapefruit and blood orange, with an underlying layer of vanilla and some char. Similar on the palate, though not overly fruity — rather, it’s on the bitter side, with lots of orange peel rather than juice. A drizzle of sesame and some brown butter give the finish a lift, but the experience is otherwise straightforward and never able to get much beyond its citrusy roots — nor does it seem overly intent on trying to. 100 proof. B / $70

Lasso Motel Single Barrel Rye Cask Strength 10 Years Old Review

A racy rye from MGP — 95% rye, 5% barley, bottled at full strength (which varies by bottle). Classic rye spice kicks things off: The nose here is green and peppery, with layers of ginger, orange peel, and grapefruit abutting sweeter aromas of dates and prunes — those latter elements becoming much more visible with some time in glass. Layers of cinnamon become particularly present after that. The palate follows a similar trajectory, starting off with a heavy emphasis on punchy grass and pepper notes before moving into sweeter territory: nut butter, heavy on the almonds, and some dark chocolate. A spray of florals winds things up. This is a complex whiskey that evolves and merits more appreciation the longer you spend with it. 122.4 proof as reviewed. A- / $90

Lasso Motel Kentucky Straight Whiskey 4 Years Old Review

This is an oddity, made from the same Green River mash as above, but not billed as a bourbon for some reason. There’s no mention of finishing here, but maybe it could have used some. The nose is very simplistic and heavy on barrel char — indistinct and largely inscrutable. The palate surprises, however, showcasing a body that is sweet and candylike, dripping with fruit — primarily cherries in syrup. Hershey’s chocolate gives the finish an unctuous quality, then a rather industrial wone. Boozy and a bit harsh, it would come across as much less approachable were it not for all the sweetness. One to skip in this lineup. 100 proof. C / $45 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Lasso Motel Kentucky Straight Whiskey 8 Years Old Review

This is not an 8-year-old version of the above but rather a distillate from Barton, 75% corn, 21% rye, and 4% malted barley — and again not billed as a bourbon. Like the 4 year old, however, it’s quite soft and easygoing, a well-tempered clavier of a whiskey that finds a nose which leans into malted milk, caramel sauce, and a lighter char that evokes sandalwood over oak. Some green underbrush makes an appearance, and a touch of soy. The palate does not take much of a diversion, supple with buttery oak and a coconut-touched character that feels very Continental. A pinch of baking spice livens up the later stages of the sip, while the finish offers a slightly bolder punch of dark chocolate and tobacco leaf. An easy sipper if not a particularly exciting one. 100 proof. B+ / $90 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Lasso Motel American Straight Whiskey 18 Years Old Review

Also not an 18-year-old version of the 4 or 8 year old whiskeys, but rather an 18 year old MGP corn whiskey made from 99% corn and 1% malted barley. It smells and tastes the part — an old, boozy combination of butterscotch, vanilla, and tons of buttered popcorn. Doughy marzipan is given a bit of nuance in the form of a sprinkle of black pepper, but the finish takes a vegetal turn, leaving things a touch sour on the back end. Old corn whiskey can be something of an acquired taste with its sweet, moonshiny attack, and this strays only little from expectations. 121 proof. B / $130 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Lasso Motel James Dean Rye Whiskey 13 Years Old Review

James Dean died over 70(!) years ago but his spirit lives on at Lasso Motel in the form of, oddly, a rye whiskey with some serious age. This is a very aggressive 95% rye/5%  barley MGP rye, complex and quite heady on the nose with intense herbal elements bound with aromas of anise and fennel, later tea leaf and clove. A black pepper and bay leaf character builds from there, alongside flowery saffron and sweeter butterscotch. Tons going on, most of it in relative sync. The palate sees a rush of up-front anise tempered by notes of citrus and some green tea, while the finish showcases the spices and herbs in attendance. Hard-edged thanks to a bracing abv, but with plenty to offer if you’re willing to put in the time to investigate. 112 proof. A- / $160 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: Whiskeys of Lasso Motel (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.

title: Review: Aguita Magica Ensemble Mezcal
summary:

It also has “magica” in the name. All of that aside, this ensemble release is made from a blend of 7-year old Espadín and…

The post Review: Aguita Magica Ensemble Mezcal appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
This quirky mezcal from Oaxaca’s Don Rogelio comes packaged in a conical bottle, wrapped in gold wire, with upside-down language on parts of the label — so, you see, it’s special. It also has “magica” in the name.

All of that aside, this ensemble release is made from a blend of 7-year old Espadín and 15-year(!) old Tobalá agaves, made with a traditional tahona and cooked in underground ovens.

We received a small sample to review — and even the mini was wrapped in gold wire.

Aguita Magica Ensemble Mezcal Review

The nose surprises with its general softness, the smoke well-tamed and the aroma otherwise somewhat indistinct. It takes its time to develop, at which point notes of freshly turned earth, mushroom, and green bean arrive, layered with notes of chimney soot. Things sweeten up with time in glass, showcasing a curious blend of lime leaf bubbling away in brown butter, peppery on the back end.

The producer notes banana as the predominant tasting note, and it’s a curious one that has had me noodling over it. Plantain, I think, is more accurate, with its starchy, more savory character — here coming across as less cooked than you’d expect with your Cuban dinner. The smoke isn’t heavy, but it’s certainly present, more gravelly and tarry than I expected (or desired) given the curiously fruity attack. As the mezcal develops a significant minerality develops, like licking a freshly cut piece of slate. A more savory quality builds from there, the finish evoking smoked nopales, street corn, and more tough, wet asphalt.

Initially gentle and almost innocuous, this is a mezcal that develops gradually, forcefully, and almost bizarrely as it falls ass-first down its bespoke rabbit hole, landing on a nutty and candy-sweet pillow at the bottom. While it’s an enchanting experience from start to finish, in the end I couldn’t decide whether I wanted more brooding smokiness out of it… or less.

80 proof. NOM-O638X.

B+ / $70 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Remus Lou Gehrig Reserve Bourbon
summary:
Can the folks at Remus leave dead baseball players alone even for a minute? After Babe Ruth got his due — with two release so far — now Lou Gehrig is the recipient of the ultimate reward for solid hitting and fielding on the diamond: His own namesake bourbon. There’s plenty to unpack in this…

The post Review: Remus Lou Gehrig Reserve Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Can the folks at Remus leave dead baseball players alone even for a minute? After Babe Ruth got his due — with two release so far — now Lou Gehrig is the recipient of the ultimate reward for solid hitting and fielding on the diamond: His own namesake bourbon.

There’s plenty to unpack in this release, which is made with four mashbills designed to honor Gehrig’s jersey number (#4), and a 109-proof bottling level to pay homage to his 109 RBIs hit in 1926… the 100th anniversary of the whiskey’s release. 9,665 bottles of Remus Lou Gehrig Reserve will be released, commemorating Gehrig’s lifetime total plate appearances. As with the Babe Ruth releases, a QR code on the back of each bottle letting you look up what happened. At my bottle’s game (which included at-bat sample #8,594), he went 1 for 5, so… not the best.

The four mashbills deserve a deeper dive, including:

  • 14% 2016 bourbon with a 44% rye mashbill
  • 70% 2017 bourbon with a 49% rye mashbill
  • 8% 2019 bourbon with a 99% corn mashbill
  • 8% 2019 bourbon with a 36% rye mashbill

There’s some old stuff in here, it seems. So let’s see if it’s a hit or a strikeout.

Remus Lou Gehrig Reserve Bourbon Review

Really pretty nose here: Nutty, with lots of cinnamon and nutmeg. A caramel corn element is present but not overly dominant, which is perhaps not surprising considering how much rye is in the overall mashbill here. Time in glass allows a toasted marshmallow note to develop along with a more subtle marzipan character — all told the pastry shop vibe is, kind of surprisingly, in full effect.

The palate shows a little more nuance. Sweet and laden with baking spice up top, the whiskey soon develops a slightly more verdant bent, showing notes of fresh cedar and a burst of mint. Increasingly chocolatey and spicy as it develops, the finish eventually approaches a Mexican chocolate vibe, with a reprise of marshmallow, almond, and more milk chocolate elements.

I have to say, this was not really what I was expecting — but hey, that’s baseball.

109 proof.

B+ / $130 [BUY IT NOW FROM RESERVEBAR]

title: Best Single Malt Scotch Under $100 (Updated 2026)

The post Best Single Malt Scotch Under $100 (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Single malt Scotch occupies a rare place in the drinking world, and rightly so. Considered by many to be the king of all whiskeys, these spirits made from 100% malted barley in chilly Scotland, where they commonly require a decade or more to mature, offer a drinking experience that offers time to enjoy, to analyze, to reflect.

Stylistically, single malt Scotch ranges immensely, defined by five (or six, depending on how you count) regions within this small country. Unlike with, say, the best bourbons or the top Irish whiskeys, answer the question of “what’s the best Scotch I can get for $X” is an extremely loaded question, the answer driven heavily by the tastes of your friend.

We’re going to try anyway, and we’re setting a cap of $100 for this list of over a dozen of the best single malts on the market, all hand-selected and approved by Drinkhacker’s reviewing staff.

First, some ground rules: Remember, we are only looking at single malt Scotch — 100% barley whiskies made entirely by one distillery. There are plenty of great sub-$100 blended Scotch whiskies out there, but we’ll look at those for a future roundup.

Next, the $100 limit is a strict one. As we did with our top bourbon lists, we used the average U.S. price of each spirit as reported by wine-searcher to determine if the whisky qualified for this guide. (Those prices, as of press time, are reported below.) Will you find these whiskies available for more or less than the price below? Absolutely. And if you find deals, you should pick them up!

As with our other lists, we are also including only full-time permanent releases. Special editions or periodic releases aren’t eligible — though rarely will you find any of those available for $100 anyway.

Want more Scotch coverage? Drop us a line and tell us what you’re looking for — malts, blends, different price caps? We’re listening, and will be back with additional looks at this market — and updates to this list — down the road.

Note: This is not a ranked list. Selections are presented in no particular order.

13 Top Single Malt Scotch Whiskies Under $100

Lagavulin 16 Years Old

Lag 16 scrapes onto the honor roll at just under $100, and one suspects by the next edition it will have been shown the door, with inflation, fashion, or simple attrition showing no respect to reputation. This Islay malt speaks bluntly, in the manner of someone who has stopped bothering to be liked: iodine, tar, and a maritime severity suggesting less a distillery than a cold coastline. Smoke, charred meat, lemon, and a trace of sherry join the argument without ever softening it. It’s a brutish, unyielding dram, suited to those who prefer conviction to comfort. It is best enjoyed slowly, in poor light, while contemplating decisions no longer open for revision. Strictly based on the numbers, this is likely the oldest (good) age-statemented whisky you can get for under 100 bucks today. Also note: The 11 year old expression is an excellent value. 86 proof. -RS $97 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Glenmorangie “The Original” 12 Years Old

The least expensive whisky on this list at just $45 (at press time), Glenmo’s “The Original” recently undertook a rare move, pushing its age statement from 10 to 12 years of age. It remains an icon of the single malt world and an archetype of what Glenmorangie is all about – delicately fruity, gently spicy, lightly floral, a whisky designed for springtime sips, easy cocktails, and abject versatility. The Original is a crowd-pleaser unlike many others in the world of Scotch, something that rank novices can enjoy alongside veteran maltheads. 80 proof. $45  [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Bruichladdich The Classic Laddie

Bruichladdich’s flagship malt states its case by refusing the usual Islay customs entirely: an absence of peat, smoke and theatrical brooding. Only barley speaking clear and plain, which is a policy so contrarian on the Islay coast it toes the line into heresy. What emerges is bright, almost cheerful: honeyed malt, lemon, pear and a floral lift suggesting spring rain rather than coastal storm. Where its neighbors traffic in gravity and unrepentant austerity, this one trades in optimism and approachability, and does so without apology: a major reason why there’s always an open bottle standing ready on our home bar cart. 100 proof. -RS $59 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Loch Lomond 12 Years Old

Regardless of expression, Loch Lomond regularly handles its business with little fanfare. But the 12 year old certainly deserves inclusion on this list for its remarkable quality-to-price ratio. Orchard fruit, lemon meringue and a sweet cream biscuit run throughout before a finish of baking spice and tobacco slowly recedes. What helps to distinguish the dram is arithmetic: a whisky of complexity priced as though it weren’t. It’s a nice instance of the market undervaluing something performing above its suggested retail price. Start here and dig deeper into its impressive portfolio. 92 proof. -RS $49 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Glen Scotia 15 Years Old

Glen Scotia flies well under the radar, but smart shoppers know there’s amazing value and quality to be found in the Campbeltown-based distillery’s line. Woody but not overblown, the whisky reaches into territory that’s more familiar to Speyside, with brown sugar and baking spice atop gentle fruit, but time in glass reveals at least some of this unique locations charms in the form of a gentle maritime note and an edge of smoky tobacco. Oily and unctuous, it’s arguably the best whisky in the Glen Scotia portfolio (better than the 18 year old, even). 92 proof. $93 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Laphroaig 10 Years Old

While Laphroaig’s reputation is one of intense peatiness, pepper, iodine, and saline – all the trappings of Islay – in reality it’s a much more approachable dram than you’d expect. You can thank a significant sweetness for that, a heavy fruit character that swirls berries and raisins into the proceedings. Peat in fact is more elegant and well-integrated into the picture, leading to a finish that sees its smokiness dusted with a honeyed, maple-adjacent character. It’s certainly not a whisky I’d hand to a Scotch novitiate, but it has far more general appeal than you might expect. $62 [BUY IT NOW FROM THE WHISKY EXCHANGE] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Ardbeg Uigeadail

You can absolutely pick up the classic Ardbeg 10 Years Old for well under $100, but if you want to step up (while still staying under the $100 limit), pick up Uigeadail instead. Named for Ardbeg’s own on-property lock, this whisky is made with older stock (though it carries no age statement) and includes aging in both bourbon and sherry casks. The sherry really changes the tone of the whisky, taking the damp smokiness of Ardbeg 10 and infusing it with nutty, citrusy, and more leathery elements that dramatically enhance the complexity of the experience. It’s also quite a bruiser at over 54% abv – and worth every penny. 108.4 proof. $93 [BUY IT NOW FROM THE WHISKY EXCHANGE] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Talisker 10 Years Old

Talisker is the only major distillery on the Isle of Skye, which makes this 10 year old offering pretty much the only sub-$100 whisky you’ll find from the island. Talisker blurs the line between peaty Islay and the mainland, and the distillery’s entry-level age-stated dram serves as a useful primer for the style. Fruit and smoke walk hand in hand, with notes of spice, shortbread, and maritime seaweed weaving in and out. It’s a young whisky but an exuberant one that works really well as part of a “tour of Scotland” tasting, offering a unique flavor profile that you won’t find repeated elsewhere. Sadly, only a few years ago you could nab this for under $50. Things have changed quickly. 91.6 proof. $74 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

GlenDronach Original 12 Years Old

GlenDronach is another classic Scotch brand – dating back to 1826 – that flies well under the radar among most Scotch drinkers. That’s a mistake, because the distillery is a gem, producing heavily sherried single malts (including both oloroso and Pedro Ximenez, unheard of at this price level) almost across the board that stand out in a sea of bourbon barrel-aged competitors. Oily, woody, and delightfully citrusy, the entry-level 12 year old is both austere and seductive, with a sherry-fueled finish that lingers just about forever. Sherry bomb lovers, look no further. 86 proof. $74 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Speyburn 15 Years Old

Speyburn is one of the most iconic single malts when it comes to getting bang for your buck, and while its 10 year old expression is a decent dram, you’ll do far better by upgrading to the 15 year old option, one of only a handful of whiskies that can offer a 15 year old age statement for under 100 bucks. That said, there’s no huge surprise in store for you here, and Speyburn 15 presents itself appropriately as a bourbon barrel-aged offering with a light finish in sherry casks, that finishing run showing itself most clearly on the whisky’s slightly sharp, citrusy palate. Some spice and oily walnut notes on the finish round everything out. 92 proof. $74 [BUY IT NOW FROM THE WHISKY EXCHANGE] [BUY IT NOW FROM RESERVEBAR] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Glenfarclas 12 Years Old

If you want a good deal on some very old Scotch, Glenfarclas has long been the go-to brand to check out. While the deals on well-aged Glenfarclas aren’t quite what they used to be, you can still find Glenfarclas 21 for about $220, and Glenfarclas 40 for under $1400. (Compare to Glenfiddich 40 for about $5200.) The 12 year old remains a classic, buttery and cereal-forward up top, its sherry finishing adding a twist of orange peel that works well with its malty, nutty, often gingery palate. Pricing isn’t what it used to be, but the value is still more than decent. The 10 year old expression is equally solid. 86 proof. $77 [BUY IT NOW FROM TOTAL WINE] [BUY IT NOW FROM THE WHISKY EXCHANGE] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Picture 412

The Macallan Sherry Oak Cask 12 Years Old

There aren’t many Macallan expressions available for under $100. This one’s definitely your best bet, and it’s an iconic example of Macallan’s house style: Boldly sherried, nutty, and quite intense. It’s a rather leathery whisky, still rather youthful and finding its feet, with ample notes of malty cereal and a sharp edge of oak. That said, it’s a definitive crowd-pleaser, particularly as it opens up in glass to showcase what 12 long years in a Spanish sherry cask can do to a spirit. 86 proof. $93 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Tamdhu 12 Years Old

As recently as 2013 Tamdhu was shut down, and it’s been wiggling its way back into the whisky zeitgeist ever since. A distillery with deep expertise and a solid range of value-priced offerings, Tamdhu’s 12 year old expression is a nice step up from the 10 year old, but still well under $100 on the shelf. Aged fully in oloroso sherry casks, this is another boldly wine-forward whisky that balances oily, nutty, and citrusy elements with more soothing notes of baking spice and pastry dough. Refreshing, with a gentle salinity on the outro. 86 proof. $69 [BUY IT NOW FROM RESERVEBAR] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Bonus Option: Kirkland & Trader Joe’s Single Malts

We’ve been fortunate to have reviewed the privately bottled single malt whiskeys available at Costco and Trader Joe’s on a number of occasions, and while they aren’t always 100% hits, they’re usually extreme deals. Case in point: Only a few years ago we picked up a 22 year old Kirkland bottling for all of $80, unheard of in the world of official distillery bottlings. The catch? The distillery is almost never revealed on the label, and while many bottles hint strongly at the identity of the distiller, that’s not always the case – especially for the Kirkland releases. These whiskies are something of a revolving door for these retailers, and you never know what is going to be in stock (or if any single malts are going to be on the shelf at all). But more often than not, the ones you do find are more than worth the asking price, even if having a Kirkland-branded whisky on your shelf isn’t much for bragging rights. (And at the very least, speculating about their origin is great fun.) Proof and prices vary.

title: Review: Grey Goose Berry Rouge Vodka
summary:

The post Review: Grey Goose Berry Rouge Vodka appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Its Essences aside, it’s been nearly 15 years since we last encountered a flavored Grey Goose expression. That changes today with a look at Grey Goose Berry Rouge, which is flavored with a mix of berry flavors — strawberry, raspberry, blackberry, and blueberry — all from “the sun-kissed fields of the Mediterranean.”

That’s about all we know (and more than most vodka producers are likely to tell you), so let’s dive in.

Grey Goose Berry Rouge Vodka Review

Appropriately, the nose of this vodka is bold with berry aromas, though there’s an ethanol underbelly that keeps any overt fruitiness in check. Blackberry and raspberry are seemingly the most immersive on the nose, but given the fruit salad construction of the spirit, it’s hard to pin anything down with any real specificity.

The palate feels brighter than the darker fruit that infuses the nose. Here, strawberry dominates, with raspberry playing second fiddle. A modest vanilla tone keeps everything in check and gives the vodka a wholly appropriate dessert-like character. This isn’t a spirit for martinis, of course, but it slides right into place in a cosmo or as the lead role in a long drink made with soda or another fizzy mixer. It finishes with a surprising cleanliness, stuffed with crushed berries while also offering a curious, lingering touch of fresh pear juice.

It’s not the sort of thing I personally tend to mix cocktails up with, but even I can’t complain about how balanced and generally delightful the Berry Rouge experience is.

80 proof.

A- / $26

title: Review: Bardstown Bourbon Co. Lochs of Jura Barrel Finish
summary:
For their latest Barrel Finish release (formerly the Collaborative Series), Bardstown Bourbon Co. explored the impact of traditional single malt casks on one of their bespoke blends of well-aged bourbon and rye whiskey. We’re having plenty of conversations these days about American single malt, but the use of traditional single malt casks to finish American…

The post Review: Bardstown Bourbon Co. Lochs of Jura Barrel Finish appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
For their latest Barrel Finish release (formerly the Collaborative Series), Bardstown Bourbon Co. explored the impact of traditional single malt casks on one of their bespoke blends of well-aged bourbon and rye whiskey. We’re having plenty of conversations these days about American single malt, but the use of traditional single malt casks to finish American whiskeys is a somewhat rarer concept. When it has been done, peated whiskey casks from Islay have often been the preferred choice for the unmistakable smoky character they impart. Bardstown Bourbon Co., however, was apparently not looking for smoke when it selected the casks for this release from the lone distillery on the Isle of Jura.

The Jura Distillery sits just across a narrow waterway from Islay, home to some of the world’s best-known peated whisky makers, but Jura itself uses little to no peat in its production. A small peated component was incorporated into its program in 2018, presumably predating the filling of the ex-bourbon and ex-sherry casks that eventually made their way to Bardstown for this release. For a whopping 32 months, those Jura casks held a bespoke bou-rye blend: 70% Indiana- and Kentucky-sourced bourbon blended with 30% Indiana-sourced rye (the 95/5 kind), all aged between 10 and 12 years. This one has generated plenty of buzz already this year, so let’s see what all the fuss is about.

Bardstown Bourbon Co. Lochs of Jura Barrel Finish Review

This is immediately an engaging and unusual bourbon. And it’s one of the more nuanced Bardstown Bourbon Co. finishes I’ve tasted, delivering layers of complexity that emerge the longer it sits in the glass. The nose is honeyed and malty, with top notes of dried currants, lemon peel, and barley sugar. The rye-forward bourbon blend is expressive, offering citrus, dried herbs, peppercorn, and even the telltale dilly notes you often find in 95/5 rye. But laced throughout that somewhat familiar bouquet is an equally expressive Scotch dimension, layering on notes of nougatine, oatmeal raisin cookies, and warm barley to create something altogether unique and memorable.

The palate delivers a noticeable malt influence right away, with dense, biscuity notes of brown sugar oatmeal, gingersnaps, and Christmas cake. It’s not a scorcher in terms of proof, but there’s plenty of peppery warmth, especially on the midpalate, where the bou-rye blend complements those malty notes with clove, cinnamon, and subtler pickling spice. The diversity of oak is nicely integrated, as well, with the chocolate and vanilla notes of the bourbon and rye barrels melding with softer hints of nutty sherry, wood smoke, and old dunnage from the Scotch casks.

This isn’t a shy whiskey, despite its modest proof, with a budding sweetness and spice that builds across the sip. Toffee and Fig Newton notes on the midpalate become increasingly honeyed and sugary on the long finish, adding intensity to a final flourish of baking spice and fading notes of graham cracker, marmalade, and Cracker Jacks that linger with an easy warmth. Lochs of Jura Barrel Finish nails the fusion of New and Old World whiskeys. The hype is very real.

104 proof.

A / $140 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Wines of Joseph Phelps’ Freestone, 2026 Releases
summary:
Earlier this year, Joseph Phelps released its single vineyard expressions, all crafted at and named for its Freestone estate, to the public. Previously these wines were only available to wine club members via allocation, but the shifting realities of the wine market seems to have opened up some wiggle room in the form of broader,…

The post Review: Wines of Joseph Phelps’ Freestone, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Earlier this year, Joseph Phelps released its single vineyard expressions, all crafted at and named for its Freestone estate, to the public. Previously these wines were only available to wine club members via allocation, but the shifting realities of the wine market seems to have opened up some wiggle room in the form of broader, better access.

Here Phelps explains what Freestone is all about:

Freestone’s wines are defined by two distinct estate vineyards: Pastorale and Quarter Moon. Each site, nestled on the fog-swept, rugged edge of the Sonoma Coast, possesses a unique terroir that imparts singular characteristics. The vineyards benefit from persistent coastal fog, sculpting winds, and soils shaped by ancient marine sediments, creating a micro-climate unlike any other. The vineyard-designate bottlings capture each site with clarity and precision, offering nuanced expression that reveals the profound influence of this unique Sonoma Coast terroir. These are pure, site-driven wines of remarkable specificity.

Winemaker Justin Ennis crafts Freestone wines with a deep attention to detail, capturing the distinct character of each vineyard while balancing the vibrancy of the terroir with a refined, elegant structure. Now, that deep-rooted vision comes to market, as Justin and the winery introduce these vineyard-driven wines to a broader audience for the first time.

Today we look at three Freestone bottlings. And, for comparison’s sake, we’re including a look at a Joseph Phelps-branded version of what seems to be one of the same wines.

2024 Freestone Chardonnay Estate Grown Sonoma Coast – Bright notes of coconut and lemon create an iconic Sonoma chardonnay experience, the wine’s creaminess giving the experience a custard/pie-like quality from the jump. There’s no mistaking this wine’s character — it tells you exactly what it is from start to finish — but it does so with finesse. Never dripping with vanilla or heavy with oakiness, it remains effusive and bright, taking a slightly tropical bent on the finish that touches on guava and a hint of brighter pineapple adding some much-needed acidity. As outstanding a chardonnay as you’ll find from California these days. A / $50

2023 Freestone Pinot Noir West Sonoma Coast – Fruit-forward but short of jammy, this expressive wine bursts with blackberry and raspberry notes before sliding into gently herbal territory, evoking notes of tea leaf, bay leaf, and rosemary. As the finish approaches, a gentle chocolate note develops, though loads of acidity keep this wine bright and effusive, never delving into overt notes of earthy savoriness. Instead, layers of cinnamon and ginger give the conclusion a surprisingly holiday-friendly vibe, the wine remaining fully alive throughout its lengthy and lightly tart denouement. Outstanding pinot. A / $125

2023 Freestone Pinot Noir Sonoma Coast – One would think the Sonoma Coast and West Sonoma Coast expressions from the same vintage would have a lot in common, but this wine is intense in ways that I didn’t expect. Powerful notes of anise and turned earth open the door to a very savory experience, with elements of green beans and roast beef adding even more to the dusky-husky experience. It isn’t until the finish that a layer of inky black fruit finally develops, notes of extracted blackberry and blueberry providing a much-needed counterpoint (if only just so) to what can be an almost overwhelming experience for a pinot noir. B / $77

2023 Joseph Phelps Freestone Vineyards Pinot Noir Sonoma Coast – Immediately similar to the Freestone bottling, and for good reason, but far from a doppelganger: This is less overtly punchy, with a more restrained earthiness and less overt herbaceousness on display. It’s still intense and infused with notes of dark chocolate, coffee, and a crushed slate character, the palate moving into notes of kalamata olive before brightening up with the same blackberry/blueberry compote note that the Freestone expression showcases. The wine finishes on a quite tart note, though unlike with the above wine, it doesn’t entirely need the rush of acidity to clean things up. A- / $50

title: Review: Laphroaig Willem 14 Years Old
summary:
We’ve seen it plenty with tequila, a bit with bourbon and rum, and now Scotch brands are having their celebrity moment. Nick Offerman’s partnership with Lagavulin seems to have really kicked off the trend back in 2019. Harrison Ford’s team up with Dr. Bill and Highland darling Glenmorangie has gotten the lion’s share of publicity…

The post Review: Laphroaig Willem 14 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We’ve seen it plenty with tequila, a bit with bourbon and rum, and now Scotch brands are having their celebrity moment. Nick Offerman’s partnership with Lagavulin seems to have really kicked off the trend back in 2019. Harrison Ford’s team up with Dr. Bill and Highland darling Glenmorangie has gotten the lion’s share of publicity this year. Meanwhile, Laphroaig’s celebrity collaboration with actor Willem Dafoe, which has been in the works since late 2025, has been as understated and eclectic as the man himself.

The whisky that resulted from this unlikely partnership debuted this past spring. It’s a 14-year-old single malt initially aged in ex-bourbon casks before a nine-month finishing in oloroso sherry casks. Full maturation in oloroso has yielded some real gems for the brand, but finished expressions haven’t always been our favorite Laphroaigs. Mr. Dafoe freely admitted that he couldn’t quite articulate the flavors he’d found in this whisky and chose it as much for the curiosity it inspired as how it tasted. Keeping with that theme, Laphroaig didn’t even bother to provide their own tasting notes, describing it in the press release as “deliberately unexplained.” Consider our interest thoroughly piqued!

Laphroaig Willem 14 Years Old Review

Curious is a good way to describe the aroma. It’s at once classically Laphroaig with its brine and medicinal funk but then altogether meatier and fruitier in turns. On the nose, the coastal hallmarks of the brand are kept at bay beneath a sweet, mesquite smoke and dry, dusty minerality. The aroma is redolent with barbecue brisket, coal ash, and a bit of burned barbecue sauce. A slight salinity shows itself as it blooms along with some seaweed before giving way to grilled lemon and eventually overcooked berry cobbler and oxidized wine.

The palate showcases some of the same tension but with an unusual amount of sweetness for Laphroaig, beginning with rich Demerara syrup and holiday spice before adding currants and fig jam across the sip. The midpalate attempts to rein in some of the sweetness, introducing a nice contrasting salinity with undertones of mesquite smoke and oyster shells. That moderation is short-lived, however, as marzipan, coffee syrup, and sugary raisin arrive on the finish and linger with subtler, meaty (but still sweet) notes of candied bacon and barbecue burnt ends. Like Willem, I’m not sure I entirely know what to think of this whisky. It’s too sweet to be considered a classic Laphroaig, but it carries that sweetness far better than the younger Sherry Oak release. With the proper disclaimers, it’s certainly worth exploring for fans of the brand. And it could even be a good gateway into Islay whisky for the more peat averse Scotch drinker.

107.4 proof.

B+ / $156 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Tally Tumbler Golf 20 Oz
summary:
The latest contender in the category of “things I never knew I needed” could be the Tally Tumbler, which is a literal twist on the ubiquitous insulated drink containers. Per their website, the Tally Tumbler is “a scorekeeping tumbler built for golf, backyard games, tailgates, and recreational play. It helps you track scores without using…

The post Review: Tally Tumbler Golf 20 Oz appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The latest contender in the category of “things I never knew I needed” could be the Tally Tumbler, which is a literal twist on the ubiquitous insulated drink containers. Per their website, the Tally Tumbler is “a scorekeeping tumbler built for golf, backyard games, tailgates, and recreational play. It helps you track scores without using a phone, paper scorecard, or separate counter.” 

To have any shot in a saturated market, it first needs to pass muster and hold its own in a rather crowded field of top rated insulated drink containers. It should fit in most cupholders, be sturdily made and keep drinks cold or hot for a reasonable period of time.  

It’s time to tee up a round of their 20 ounce Gold Tumbler. 

The base of the Tally Golf is approximately 2.86 inches wide and fits nicely with the most common cupholder measurements, which are typically 2.6 to 3.0 inches. But more relevantly, it fit comfortably in my husband’s golf bag, and that seemed to unequivocally settle the matter. 

The materials, construction, and feel of the Tally stands up solidly to its peers. There is great weight and good grip on the finish. 

For insulation, I applied the “overnight ice” test which is to fill the test subject with ice and leave it overnight on the kitchen counter. The Tally preserved two-thirds of the ice after 10 hours. The equivalent “forgotten coffee” test resulted in similar respectable duration. I filled it with coffee at 186 degrees, and after 4 hours it cooled to 124 degrees. (Caveat: the top was completely sealed, so with recurring sips, expect greater heat loss.)

And now we turn to the chef’s kiss of the “tally” in the “Tally.” There are 3 rubberized rotating rings discreetly embedded at the top with various markings to track some presumably critical metrics including number of strokes, FIR (which measures driving accuracy) and GIR (which measures approach accuracy), and possibly the most underappreciated metric, number of lost balls. I’m not a golfer but I sense these details must help the recreational golfer really feel seen. 

My husband was particularly, and perhaps excessively, excited with how much time and logistical annoyance was saved by not having to pull out a piece of paper or a phone to mark scores. I could almost see the glorious visions parading in his head of finishing a hole and taking a satisfied (or frustrated?) sip from his Tally while rotating the relevant bands with the deftness of a juggling Rubic’s Cube master. Voila. On to the next hole. 

Plenty of fun colors to choose from, and they offer personalized engravings. If you want to be even more extra, you can also order one that comes with a lid that works as a Bluetooth speaker. You read that right. 

Note that the Tally requires a little more TLC than your standard rugged tumbler, and hand washing is highly recommended over tossing into the dishwasher, which doesn’t seem that big of an ask. Let’s see if we can have nice things. 

A / $36 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]
